messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Clinical Vignette: Robert

Robert was sixty-seven years old when he came to the clinic, a broad-shouldered man with the careful posture of someone accustomed to bearing weight. He had spent thirty-two years as a military medic, a career that had taught him to remain steady when others fell apart. His wife of forty years had died three years prior, and in the intervening silence of their empty house, he had begun to understand how much of his identity had been tethered to the work of keeping people alive. Now, with that chapter closed and retirement stretching before him, he found himself unable to move through the world without feeling like it might collapse beneath him.

The collision happened on a Tuesday afternoon in March, eighteen months before his first appointment. Robert had been driving to a medical supply store when a pickup truck ran a red light and struck his sedan broadside. The impact was violent and disorienting—the sound of metal crumpling, the smell of burning rubber and spilled gasoline, the taste of blood from where he had bitten his tongue. A man stumbled from the pickup truck reeking of alcohol, and in the chaos that followed, Robert found himself doing what he had always done: assessing, triaging, moving to help. But his hands would not stop shaking. By the time the ambulance arrived, he was uncertain whether he was checking the other driver's pupils or his own, whether the ringing in his ears was real or a sign that something fundamental had broken inside him.

The first weeks were physical. His ribs ached, his left shoulder throbbed, and he slept poorly. But the body heals in predictable ways. What did not heal was the way his nervous system had recalibrated itself to threat. Ordinary sounds—a car horn, a loud truck passing on the street, even the sharp bang of a kitchen cabinet closing—would jolt him upright, his heart hammering as though the collision were happening again in real time. The startle responses came unbidden and exhausting. What frightened Robert most was the sense that he could no longer trust his own mind. He had come to believe that the accident had exposed a fundamental weakness in him, that a truly strong person would have recovered by now. The fact that he still jumped at sounds, that he still felt the phantom lurch of impact when a car slowed suddenly near him, seemed to confirm what he had begun to suspect: he was not the man he had thought himself to be.

Within two months, Robert stopped driving. The thought of being behind the wheel triggered a cascade of physical sensations—his chest tightening, his palms sweating, a sharp clarity to his vision that felt almost hallucinatory. He could not be a passenger either. The moment he sat in someone else's car, he found himself monitoring the other driver's attention, tensing at every intersection, his body braced for impact. He began to construct increasingly elaborate reasons to avoid situations that would require him to be in a vehicle. He made excuses to his daughter, who had invited him to his grandson's baseball games. He stopped attending his medical society meetings. The isolation was a small price to pay for the relief of not having to face that overwhelming sense of vulnerability and shame.

But isolation had its own cost. Alone in the house, Robert's mind became a place he could not escape. When he tried to talk about what had happened—when his daughter asked him directly, her concern evident in the careful way she phrased her questions—the narrative would fragment. He would begin to describe the impact, the sound, the smell of the other driver's breath, and then something would happen to the thread of his story. His voice would falter. The memory itself seemed to split into pieces that would not cohere, as though it belonged to someone else entirely, something that had happened to a stranger rather than to him. And beneath that alienation lay something worse: the intrusive sounds. In quiet moments, he would hear the screech of tires, the crash of metal, the man's slurred voice asking if anyone was hurt. These sounds would arrive unbidden, vivid and immediate, and they would trigger another wave of physical reactivity—his heart racing, sweat on his palms, that terrible sense of helplessness.

The more Robert struggled against these intrusions, the more they intensified. He began to monitor his own thoughts obsessively, watching for signs that he was losing his grip on reality. When a memory surfaced, he would try to suppress it, to push it down through sheer force of will. But the effort of not thinking about something only tightened the loop. He would find himself hypervigilant to triggers: the smell of alcohol on a stranger's breath at the grocery store would send him into a state of alarm; the sight of a damaged car on the side of the road would trigger that cascade of physical symptoms and intrusive memories all over again. He had begun to avoid places where he might encounter these reminders—he stopped going to the grocery store at certain times, took longer routes to appointments, and when he could not avoid a trigger, he would feel the familiar tightening in his chest, the sense that the world had become fundamentally unsafe. The physical reactivity and the startle responses would follow, and then the cycle would begin again: the intrusive memories, the fragmented attempts to make sense of them, the deepening conviction that he had failed himself and could not be trusted to do the right thing. His grandson had stopped asking him to come to games. His daughter had begun to worry aloud about his isolation. And Robert, sitting in the silence of his house, had come to understand that the collision had done more than injure his body. It had shattered something essential about how he understood himself, and he had no idea how to put it back together. That was what finally brought him to the clinic: not hope that he could recover, but a desperate need to understand whether the man he saw in the mirror—weak, unreliable, broken—was who he had always been, or whether something could be done to retrieve the person he used to be.
